Author: Hemerijck, Anton; Huguenot-Noël, Robin
Title: Resilient welfare states in the European Union
Abstract Note: The European welfare systems, established after the Second World War, have been under sustained attack since the late 1970s from the neoliberal drive towards a small state and from the market as the foremost instrument for the efficient allocation of scarce resources. After the 2008 financial crash, Europe's high tax and generous benefits welfare states were, once again, blamed for economic stagnation and political immobilism. If anything, however, the long decade of the Great Recession proved that the welfare state remained a fundamental asset in hard times, stabilizing the economy, protecting households and individuals from poverty, reconciling gendered work and family life, while improving the skills and competences needed in Europe's knowledge economy and ageing society. Finally, the spread of the Covid-19 pandemic has, unsurprisingly, brought back into the limelight the productive role of welfare systems in guaranteeing basic security, human capabilities, economic opportunities, and democratic freedoms.In this important contribution, Anton Hemerijck and Robin Huguenot-NoeÌl examine the nature of European welfare provision and the untruths that surround it. They evaluate the impact of the austerity measures that followed the Great Recession, and consider its future design to better equip European societies to face social change, from global competition to accelerated demographic ageing, the digitalization of work and climate change

Author: Asongu*, Simplice A.; Diop, Samba; Nnanna, Joseph
Title: HEALTH VULNERABILITY VERSUS ECONOMIC RESILIENCE TO THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC: Global Evidence
Abstract Note: The purpose of this study is to understand how countries have leveraged on their economic resilience to fight the COVID-19 pandemic. The focus is on a global sample of 150 countries. The study develops a health vulnerability index (HVI) and leverages on an existing economic resilience index (ERI) to provide four main scenarios from which to understand the problem statement, namely ‘low HVI-low ERI,’ ‘high HVI-low ERI,’ ‘high HVI-high ERI,’ and ‘low HVI-high ERI’ quadrants. Countries that have robustly fought the pandemic are those in the ‘low HVI-high ERI’ quadrant and, to a lesser extent, countries in the ‘low HVI-low ERI’ quadrant. Most European countries, namely one African country (Rwanda), four Asian countries (e.g., Japan, China, South Korea, and Thailand), and six American countries (e.g., United States, Canada, Uruguay, Panama, Argentina, and Costa Rica) are apparent in the ideal quadrant.

Author: Pereirinha, José António Correia; Pereira, Elvira
Title: Social resilience and welfare systems under COVID-19: A European comparative perspective
Abstract Note: COVID-19 and the corresponding economic lockdown and income loss for large segments of population was something unexpected for all European countries, and their welfare systems were not prepared to protect their citizens from such threats. Social resilience is becoming used in disaster risk analysis, and preferred to that of vulnerability, to refer the ability of the social entities to respond to such challenges, enabling them to cope and adjust to adverse events. It has been more recently used in the context of the European Union (EU) about COVID-19, regarding the creation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, intended to mitigate the economic and social impact of the coronavirus pandemic. The global nature of this pandemic makes possible and relevant a deeper understanding of social resilience at different levels of analysis: international, national, local and individual/household levels. This article aims to contribute to this by proposing a set of indicators of social resilience in face of COVID-19, supported in a theoretical framework developed herein, and comparing the performance of a selection of EU countries with distinct welfare system configurations, with different roles played by the government, the market, the social organizations and the families. Using comparable statistical data at macro level and data concerning the responses of government to the economic and social effects of the pandemic, we produce a synthetic index of social resilience, combining resilience on coping and resilience on adapting. We relate the differences found in coping and adapting with the welfare system configurations of these countries.
Short Title: Social resilience and welfare systems under COVID-19

Author: Daly, Mary
Title: Revising the concept of resilience for application in a familial and low-income context
Abstract Note: This chapter's guiding interests are in the concept of resilience and its application to understand family-related behaviours and exigencies in situations of low resources. The overall goal is to review and, as necessary, revise the concept from a family and social policy perspective. Resilience is a very popular concept, seen to pick up on the need for agency and adaptation in situations of shock as defining features of contemporary and future life. The chapter proceeds by identifying the core features of resilience as a concept before moving on to interrogate its utility in highlighting important aspects of family life. The particularities, including strengths and weaknesses, of the originating literature on resilience are exposed. The discussion queries the most widely understood notion of resilience as the capacity to achieve positive outcomes in the face of adversity, and proposes a more refined and socially embedded conceptualization. A number of bodies of literature are brought together in this endeavour, especially those exploring the nature of family life, the meaning and practice of care-related responsibilities, the role and management of different types of resources in a low-resource context, and the role of social policy and the state. A common theme throughout this chapter is that, although resilience helps to reveal important aspects of the subject, it must be significantly refined to have an application to human relationships and family life in social settings.

Author: Daly, Mary
Title: Conclusion to Families, Welfare States and Resilience
Abstract Note: This book has the aim to reveal the risks that families with low resources face, examine the strategies they use to cope, and identify the resources they need to be or remain resilient. The eight preceding chapters have engaged with the concept of resilience, set out the broader European context in which families strive for resilience, and examined practices and behaviours in Belgium, Croatia, Poland, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. This chapter undertakes a comparative overview, bringing together the findings from the individual countries to draw overall conclusions. The design, methodology and scale of the study mean that there are serious limitations on the extent to which it is possible to identify robust cross-national variations (see the Introduction). Caution is called for because of the variation among focus groups at national level, which means that the national-level evidence is not a single case. However, it is possible to identify patterns. The evidence for this chapter is mainly drawn from the six preceding country chapters but is augmented by some additional evidence from the project overview report (Daly, 2024). The chapter is divided into four main sections. The first gives an overview of families in terms of the situations they experience, the meanings and significance of family, and the sources of support available. The second section paints a picture of people's engagement with the public support system and how they feel about it. In the third section, people's behaviours are placed in a context of resilience, understood in terms of the links between coping mechanisms and adaptation and change. The final section offers some thoughts on the utility of a resilience framework and resilience as a focus for social policy.

Author: Plavgo, Ilze; Hemerijck, Anton
Title: Fostering resilience: Welfare policy change across Europe between 2015 and 2019
Publication Title: Who's Afraid of the Welfare State Now?
Abstract Note: Abstract             This chapter investigates whether and in what ways European governments departed from the austerity-dominated paradigm of welfare reform after 2014. It explores the direction of change and relative coherence between the functions of social protection, activation, and capacitation, in twelve European countries, in 2015–2019. Drawing on data from national legislation, social policy reform is tracked across the life-course arenas of family policies and work–care reconciliation, lifelong education, employment, and retirement, distinguishing between regressive/exclusionary and progressive/inclusive adaptations. Overall, we observe welfare expansion and recalibration towards more integrated social investment policy mixes, especially regarding lifelong education and gender-balanced activation. This includes countries which had pursued austerity up to 2014. Nevertheless, significant cross-country variation remains in the extent to which policies have been aligned, with some pursuing a ‘synergy-oriented’ approach and others more ambivalent reform trajectories. A minority of cases remained skewed towards transfer retrenchment and deregulatory labour market flexibilization.

Author: keck, Markus; Sakdapolrak, Patrick
Title: WHAT IS SOCIAL RESILIENCE? LESSONS LEARNED AND WAYS FORWARD
Abstract Note: [Over the last decade, a growing body of literature has emerged which is concerned with the question of what form a promising concept of social resilience might take. In this article we argue that social resilience has the potential to be crafted into a coherent analytic framework that can build on scientific knowledge from the established concept of social vulnerability, and offer a fresh perspective on today's challenges of global change. Based on a critical review of recently published literature on the issue, we propose to define social resilience as being comprised of three dimensions: 1. Coping capacities —the ability of social actors to cope with and overcome all kinds of adversities; 2. Adaptive capacities — their ability to learn from past experiences and adjust themselves to future challenges in their everyday lives; 3. Transformative capacities — their ability to craft sets of institutions that foster individual welfare and sustainable societal robustness towards future crises. Viewed in this way, the search for ways to build social resilience — especially in the livelihoods of the poor and marginalized — is revealed to be not only a technical, but also a political issue. Innerhalb der vergangenen Dekade ist eine Vielzahl von Artikeln erschienen, die sich mit der Frage beschäftigen, wie ein der Forschung dienliches Konzept von sozialer Resilienz aussehen könnte. Wir argumentieren, dass ein in sich kohärentes Forschungsprogramm erstellt werden kann, welches nicht nur in der Lage ist, Ergebnisse aus der Verwundbarkeitsforschung aufzunehmen, sondern gleichsam neue Wege für die Erforschung aktueller Problemlagen aufzuzeigen vermag. Vor dem Hintergrund der gegenwärtigen Literaturlage schlagen wir eine Definition sozialer Resilienz vor, welche drei Dimensionen umfasst: 1. Die Fähigkeit sozialer Akteure zur Bewältigung von Krisen. 2. Das Vermögen, aus vergangenen Erfahrungen zu lernen und sich an zukünftige Entwicklungen anzupassen. 3. Die Befähigung zur sozialen und ökologischen Transformation, welche das individuelle Wohlergehen fördern und einer nachhaltigen gesellschaftlichen Stärkung im Umgang mit zukünftigen Krisen dienlich sind. In dieser Betrachtungsweise erscheint die Suche nach Resilienz — insbesondere für die Lebenshaltung der Armen und Ausgegrenzten — nicht als technische, sondern primär als politische Aufgabe.]

Author: Kurowska, Anna; Kasperska, Agnieszka; Daly, Mary
Title: Families with low resources striving for resilience in Poland
Abstract Note: This chapter offers insights into the struggles faced by families in Poland (particularly those living with low resources) and the resilience strategies they adopt to cope with adverse socio-economic conditions and weaknesses of the welfare state. These are treated as resilience-oriented behaviours or strategies, understood in the context of the family seeking to find ways of keeping going in both everyday circumstances and conditions of transition, risk or challenge. The research was carried out as part of the rEUsilience project. The evidence presented is drawn from seven focus groups, involving 70 participants in total, conducted in Poland between March and April 2023. The focus groups were undertaken in various locations across the country, including one in a small town and the remainder in larger urban centres and regional capitals (i.e. voivodeship cities). The focus groups were organized to cover the experience of different family situations and living circumstances, and included low-income families, lone parents, families with female breadwinners, Ukrainian migrants, and families with heavy care responsibilities. The majority of participants were women, making up two-thirds of the sample. Most participants (64 per cent) were aged between 36 and 55. Approximately one-fifth (21 per cent) were between 18 and 25 years old; people aged 55 and over comprised 13 per cent of the sample. A significant number of participants were either engaged in low-wage jobs or had previous experience in such employment. Examples of these roles include cleaning, construction work, positions in restaurants or retail, delivery services and factory jobs.

Author: Gijbels, Eef; Uzunalioğlu, Merve; Bartova, Alzbeta; Lancker, Wim Van
Title: Families with low resources striving for resilience in Belgium
Abstract Note: This chapter draws on qualitative evidence gathered from focus groups with families in Belgium as part of the rEUsilience project. The participating families are all low-resourced and face a complex interplay of risks and constraints as they balance paid work and care-giving responsibilities. The lack of knowledge about families in these types of situation highlights the urgent need to understand how families navigate competing demands under conditions of limited resources. Understanding these dynamics is crucial not only for interpreting the lived realities of low-income families but also for grasping the broader implications of societal change and the institutional frameworks within which families carry out their lives.

Author: Backman, Lovisa; Nieuwenhuis, Rense
Title: Families with low resources striving for resilience in Sweden
Abstract Note: this chapter examines the experiences of families with low resources in Sweden. We consider families as a nexus where the needs for family support and income protection intersect through paid work, unpaid work, income, gender and care. This enables a multidimensional view of the challenges faced by families in Sweden, and of how they adapt or are constrained to adapt. The following four questions structure the analysis: what are the developments or events in their lives that families in Sweden have to respond to? What resources do families in Sweden have available and how do they use them? What levers of change do families in Sweden have at their disposal? What are the barriers to well-being and adaptation for families in Sweden; in other words, what traps them in their situation?
